en: Nāgabuddhi, *Samājamaṇḍalopāyikā* = Tucci Collection, Vikramaśīla manuscript, immediately following the *Rahaḥpradīpa* [59’ = 1]. Homage to the Buddha!
Having paid homage to Ādinātha, whose form is non-dual gnosis,
I shall describe the limbs of the maṇḍala for the benefit of the vajra-disciples.
The maṇḍala, accomplished through both conduct (caryā) and yoga, is highly praised.
Setting aside the ritual procedures of Kriyātantra, which follow the system of all the Buddhas:
first is the purification of the site, then the appropriation of the site,
followed by the pacification of obstacles, and finally the laying down of the chalk lines.
Then follows the consecration of the site, beginning with the earth; thereafter, the procedure for the announcement.
Next is the consecration of the disciples, followed by the casting of the sky-line.
Then comes the rule for the recitation of colors and the laying down of the colored powders.
Then there is the invocation of the deities and the entry of the disciple;
the ritual for the bath and the maṇḍala, and then the consecration of the Buddhas;
thereafter the sprinkling of weapons and the offering of fees to the Guru and the deity.
Then follows the granting of permission, the ritual of dismissal,
and the extraction of the ritual stake; these are the procedures for the work of the mandala,
as taught by the twenty methods according to their respective details for one who knows the full extent.
Having drawn the dust mandala, the wise Vajrācārya [should act].
(8) Some who seek the eight siddhis enter this mandala, as do heroes who have seen the truth, as well as those practitioners who are merely imagined. (9)
Having understood their state of destitution, the Guru, inclined toward compassion,
should draw an eightfold wheel for the sake of accomplishing all the aims of the disciples—
using jewels, seeds, flowers, minerals, or likewise sands.
Indeed, with moving powders, one may likewise create a mental maṇḍala; or else,
the deposition of seed-syllables, a sign, or even the very form of the deity—
whether poured, cast, or installed— should be placed in the maṇḍala according to one's capacity.

The garland, the water, the awakened vajra and bell, then the mirror, the name, the master, and the permission— this indeed is the sequence of the empowerments. The Tathāgatas have declared that there are two kinds of masters in the Vajrayāna.
One may be primarily devoted to mantra, while another is intent upon meditation.
The yogi established in the practice of mantra is dedicated to the support of the deity;
having thereby obtained the signs, he should then draw the dust mandala.
The yogi established in the system of mantra, possessing the yoga of non-dual gnosis,
should draw a wheel resembling an illusion with a body resembling an illusion,
in cities, villages, market towns, monasteries, groves, and port cities. 16.16–17a.
One should dig the ground to the depth of a knee and gradually clear it;
having removed wood, thorns, gravel, bones, charcoal, potsherds, and so forth, one should then purify the ground on all sides.
Having made it perfectly level, one should indeed smear it with cow dung;
then, having sprinkled it with scented water, one should perform the *krūra-homa* (fierce oblation).
Reciting the mantra of Vajrasattva, the practitioner should gaze with the vajra-vision.
"Even a portion of the ground of the maṇḍala that is defective becomes purified.

However, O Lord of Secrets, the mantra practitioner who, while remaining fixed in conceptual construction, purifies the ground, does not become purified, for he is devoid of the thought of awakening (bodhicitta). (20–21)
The Procedure for Purifying the Ground.
[1] Then, having constructed a mandala pavilion adorned with canopies and the like,
one should perform the ritual appropriation of the ground accompanied by the fivefold offering.
Wearing white, unwashed garments, pure, and adorned with a clean turban, beautiful with all ornaments and anointed with fragrant unguents,
one should offer the bali-oblation three times a day according to the ritual rules for three days.
Then, for the pacification of all obstacles, the one firm in his vows should first perform the *śāntika* fire-offering according to the rules before the ten *Diṅnāgas*;
afterwards, he should have the disciple perform it in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) for the successful accomplishment of the consecration (*seka*).
The Procedure for Taking Possession of the Ground.
[2] Abiding in the samādhi of Hatred-Vajra and surrounded by the wheel of wrathful deities, the yogin should perform the warding off of obstacles at the arising of skillful means. 1.
Having meditated on the vajra at the soles of his feet, intent upon brandishing the vajra,
he dances with playful vajra-steps, uttering the fierce *hūṃ* sound with bared fangs.
His left eye is made into a moon marked by the syllable *ṭa*, and his right eye is placed as a sun marked by the syllable *a*.

Bearing the pride of the Vajra-holder, the Lord, who is compassionate by nature, should circumambulate the area of the maṇḍala ground. Driving away the hosts of the wicked, including Śakra and others together with their retinues—from the earth, the atmosphere, and other realms—he should speak as follows: (3–4)

May all those who are present—whether gods, asuras, yakṣas, rākṣasas, pretas, piśācas, apasmāras, bhūtas, ḍākinīs, male or female elders, attendants, retinues, garuḍas, kimpuruṣas, or mantra-adepts—depart elsewhere!

On this spot of earth, for the sake of fulfilling the perfect awakening of such-and-such a disciple and for the purpose of causing all sentient beings to attain unsurpassed knowledge, the great maṇḍala of Śrī Vajrasattva must be drawn by me; therefore, having heard this command of the Great Vajradhara, depart immediately! Whoever does not depart, I shall shatter his head into a hundred pieces with this blazing *hūṃ*-syllable vajra, a great and fiercely flaming wisdom-vajra.

Having recited thus three times, the mantra-practitioner, fierce with wrath, standing in the eastern direction and accompanied by the *hūṃ*-syllable mudrā, should perform the ritual applications beginning with the *ālīḍha* stance according to the rules. (5) *Ālīḍha*.
The *pratyālīḍha* and *vaiśākha* stances form the mandala.
The even-footed stance, the tortoise-footed stance, and the vajra-raising stance.
Vajravilāsa consists of a single foot;
Bhramarījāla [consists of two feet].
The lion’s stride;
the lion’s yawn;
the vajra-splitting.
The vajra-strengthening; the vajra-throwing; the vajra-dancing.
Vajrabhairava;
Vajravetālī;
Vajramudgara.
The empowerment of the Four-Faced One;
Vajrakuṇḍalin;
the manifestation of the illusion of a woman.
Vajrasphoṭana,
Mahābalotkarṣaṇa,
and Vajradaṃṣṭra.
The vajra-laugh;
the vajra-sound;
the gesture of the sword.
The mudrā of the vajra;
the mudrā of the wheel; the mudrā of the mace.
The gesture of the banner;
the gesture of the noose;
the gesture of the lotus.
The gesture of the staff;
the gesture of fearlessness;
the gesture of the goad.
The gesture of a fruit;
the gesture of a spear;
the gesture of a bow.
The gesture of drawing back an arrow;
the gesture of discharging an arrow;
the gesture of whirling a *bhiṇḍivāla* weapon.
The gesture of granting boons;
the gesture of the spear;
the gesture of the ear-ornament.
The gesture of prostration;
the vajra posture;
the gesture of meditative concentration.
The vajra-paryaṅka, the lotus-seat (padmāsana), and the sattva-paryaṅka.
The heroic posture (vīrāsana), the auspicious posture (bhadrāsana), and the squatting posture (utkaṭikāsana).
The graceful toss,
the face-to-face,
and the averted face.

Thus, having threatened the excellent hosts of Indra and the other guardians of the directions with incantations of reproach, the mantra-practitioner, who knows their true nature, should properly drive in the stakes according to the respective rules.
Taking a stake made of khadira wood measuring eight finger-breadths in length, he should proceed.
One should wrap it with a five-colored thread in the proper sequence;
having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should place it in a new vessel.
Touching the stake with the hand, one should consecrate it with the three-syllable mantra.
Having thus well-consecrated the ritual stake through the perception of the reality of conventional truth,
the wise practitioner should again perform the visualization consisting of meditative absorption according to this sequence:
OṂ SUMBHA NISUMBHA HŪṂ GṚHṆA 2 HŪṂ.
Cause them to seize! Hūṃ! Bring them here! Hoḥ! O Blessed One, King of Vidyās, hūṃ phaṭ!
Having thus drawn forth the Vināyakas by means of this wrathful form,
the wise one should pierce them all according to the ritual procedure through this application.
One should visualize the great king Vajrāmṛta as the Vajra-stake.
One should visualize the portion below the navel region as being dark like the petal of a blue lotus, with a radiance filled with garlands of flames;
and the upper part as having the form of a wrathful deity, with three faces and six arms.
Holding a vajra-hammer in one hand and a stake in the left,
the Vajra-holder, assuming the form of Nisumbha, should perform the ritual of staking with this mantra:
OṂ GHA GHA GHĀTAYA GHĀTAYA SARVADUṢṬĀN PHAṬ PHAṬ KĪLAYA KĪLAYA SARVAPĀPĀN PHAṬ PHAṬ HŪṂ HŪṂ VAJRAKĪLA VAJRADHARA ĀJÑĀPAYATI KĀYAVĀKCITTAVAJRAṂ HŪṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ PHAṬ.

Having thus dispelled the obstacles through the yoga of mental construction, the knower of mantras should again purify the obstacles according to the procedure taught in the *Śrīsaṃvara*. The Victors do not perform purifications for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings, nor for the sake of the purification of ritual action.

There is no obstacle here, nor indeed are there Māras; success is established through the absence of decline even for an eon. I do not fall into the state of Māra, nor do I succumb to lack of firmness; for the sake of firmness, I do not teach out of a desire for peace.
I shall quickly become firm for the sake of supreme, excellent enlightenment—thinking, "Whoever would accomplish me through their own pleasures, not through sufferings. (15–16)
The Procedure for Pacifying Obstacles.
[3] Thereafter, the wise preceptor, being well-composed, should together with the disciple cast the chalk-line according to this sequence. 1.

The preceptor, stationed in the western quarter (Vāruṇī), should, together with the disciple standing facing him in the eastern quarter (Aindrī), cast down the Brahma-thread here. The knower of mantras, stationed in the southern quarter (Yamya), [should do so] together with one standing in the northern quarter (Kauberī).
The disciple should correctly lay down the second Brahma-thread.
Standing in the south-eastern direction, the preceptor, facing the disciple who is indeed stationed in the north-eastern direction,
should lay down the primary thread.
Standing in that very place, the Vajrin, with the son situated in the southwest,
should cause the wise one who knows the threads to cast the southern thread.
Standing in that very place, the disciple [should do so] with the mantra-holder situated in the northwest.
One should lay down the third thread situated between the directions of Nairṛti and Vāyu.
Standing in that very place, the yogi who knows the ritual, together with the son stationed in the direction of Śiva, should subsequently lay down the fourth root-thread.
The preceptor, stationed in the southeast and endowed with the yoga of his own tutelary deity,
should cause the diagonal thread to fall by means of the practitioner stationed in the northwest.
Then, the Guru, having taken his stand in the northeast direction, [should do so] by means of one situated in the southwest.
The disciple should correctly lay down the second diagonal cord.
Recalling the body of Māyā, one should divide the door from the wheel;
the door is one-eighth of the wheel, as are the strips for the deities.
The turret (niryūha), the cheek (kapola), and the side-wing (pakṣaka) shall be equal in measure to the door;
the pedestal (vedikā) shall be half of that, and the performance area (raṅgabhūḥ) half of the pedestal.
The inner circle (garbhacakra) shall be half the measure of the root-line (mūlasūtra).
One should make it radiant with a garland of vajras and adorned with five rays of light.
Outside the inner wheel, one should draw four lines;
within, one should draw eight pillars, beautifully marked with vajras.
In that very place, there are nine chambers situated between the vajra-pillars;
the necklace (hāra) should be equal in measure to the altar (vedī), and the jeweled ground (ratnabhūmi) half of that.
Likewise, the bakulī, the kramaśīrṣa, and the ground for the outer pillars and so forth [should be arranged]. 14.
The archway (toraṇa), three times the size of the door, stands atop the pitcher-pillars;
it is joined by the *pakṣiṇī* and the *kramaśīrṣa*, resounds with the ringing of bells,
and is adorned with banners, chowries, garlands, and other ornaments.

The four corners of the mandala bear half-moons, jewels, and vajras; it is inlaid with vajra-jewels at the joints of the gates and projections. The archway has a vajra pinnacle, and outside of that is the circular wall.
The laying out of the lines is completed, enriched with rays of light like a garland of vajras;
one should arrange the others according to the proportions of the wheel and as is aesthetically pleasing.
The first [mandala] should be the size of Brahmā’s altar, and the second half the size of that altar.
The third [line] is with half the altar, and then that [subsequent part] is with half of that;
beginning from one cubit up to a thousand cubits, the mantra-practitioner should draw the maṇḍala according to the capacity of the disciple. (19)
The Procedure for Laying out the Lines with Chalk [4]:
Having then pinned down the obstructors, and having meditated upon the enclosure, the cage, and so forth, as well as the ground consisting of vajras, one should consecrate the marked-out lines. 1.
O Goddess, you are the witness of all the Buddhas, the Protectors,
regarding the specificities of the methods of conduct and the stages and perfections;
just as the power of Māra was shattered by the Protector, the Lion of the Śākyas.
Thus, having conquered the host of Māra, I shall draw the maṇḍala.
Having smeared the ground with fragrant substances and the like, and having scattered various flowers,
the wise one should construct the maṇḍala in the place of the wielders of the discus using sandalwood.
Having procured a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay— whichever is available— the observer of the vow should set it down.
[He should also place] coral, silver, gold, ruby, and pearl-oyster shell.
One should cast the five auspicious jewels into the water of the flask.
(6) Barley, wheat, beans, sesame, and likewise mung beans—these five grains, being auspicious, one should place within the belly of the flask. (7)
One should throw in the roots of five medicinal plants: *bṛhatī*, *kaṇṭakārī*, *sahadevā*, *aparājitā*, and *daṇḍotpalā*.
Likewise, [the wood of] *āmra*, *udumbara*, *aśoka*, *aśvattha*, and *nāgaja* [should be used].
One should take five sprouts to beautify the mouths of the jars.
One should wrap the necks of the jars with a large white cloth.
Upon the cloth, the one skilled in the ritual rules should place very white threads.
The wise one should draw the seed-syllable or the emblem of all the maṇḍala deities on the side of the jar, which has been consecrated with saffron and other substances; these [jars],
provided with jewels and the like, should be empowered by their respective mantras.
The wise one should place [the vessels] filled with water according to the number of deities.
The wise one should place the jars in the four corners of the mandala within the space between the Cakravāḍa mountains, and he should place one more at the entrance.
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the consecration of the jars dedicated to the deities of the earth and other elements.
[5] Thereafter, the Guru—clad in red garments and adorned with all ornaments—brandishing the vajra with pride and accompanied by the bell, [should proceed]. 1.
Having seen the Buddhas and the members of the maṇḍala stationed in the intermediate space in their proper order, with eyes wide open in wonder, one should speak these words clearly:
"Today my birth has become fruitful; today my life has become fruitful."
I shall undoubtedly become equal to the Buddhas of the three times;
with a single-minded intent as a Bodhisattva, I shall become irreversible.
There is no doubt that my birth in the family of the Tathāgatas occurs this very day.
"Today is indeed my foremost day; today is my unsurpassed sacrifice;
today is my preeminent assembly because of the invitation to all the Buddhas.
Then, having pacified those Buddhas and offered them the guest-water (*argha*), he whose intellect was purified—
Having performed worship with both external and internal offerings, one should speak as follows:
"May all the Buddhas residing in every direction take heed of me!
I, named so-and-so, shall draw the Vajra-maṇḍala."

"May all the Buddhas and others come; you shall grant this accomplishment. Then, one who possesses the yoga of the perfected stage (niṣpannakrama) should rise with pride and perform the rites of the great maṇḍala according to one's capacity.
While circumambulating and ringing the bell, the practitioner of the vow should speak thus:
"I myself am the wielder of the thunderbolt; I myself am Vajrasattva.
I am the Buddha, the Great King; I am the Vajra-holder of great power."

"I am the Lord of Yogins, the King; I am the firm Vajrapāṇi. I am the Master, the Great Vajra. O Vajrasattva, grant me accomplishment this very day! Then one should address the Buddhas born from the five Buddha families.
Having visualized them as situated in the intermediate space, one should urge them while speaking these words:
"Tomorrow, being compassionate by nature, I wish to draw the mandala out of compassion for my disciples and for the sake of honoring you."
Therefore, O Blessed One, please grant your grace to me, your devotee.
I, the Vajra-holder named so-and-so, shall paint the auspicious mandala tomorrow, according to my capacity and with proper ritual offerings.
Out of compassion for me and my disciples, you all ought to be present together in this maṇḍala.
This is the procedure for the formal request. [6]
With the intention of uplifting the world through the splendor of a universal monarch,
he should sit at the eastern gate and consecrate those to be trained.
Then, having performed the worship of the Wheel-turning King, the excellent disciple should respectfully [attend] the Guru.
Having placed a handful of flowers upon his heart, he should pray to the Bestower of Enlightenment:
“You are my teacher, O Great Hero;
I desire, O Great Lord, the firm way of the Bodhisattvas.”
Grant me the commitment; grant me the reality and the awakened mind.
"Grant me the three refuges: the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
O Protector, lead me into the supreme city of great liberation.
May all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas attend to me! I, [name], from this moment until I sit upon the seat of enlightenment, [take refuge].
I generate the supreme, unsurpassed mind of awakening (bodhicitta),
just as the Protectors of the three times have made their resolve for perfect enlightenment;
and [I undertake] the threefold training in ethical discipline and the gathering of virtuous qualities.
I firmly undertake the ethical discipline of acting for the benefit of sentient beings;
and from this day forward, I shall uphold the vow born of the yoga of the Buddha, toward the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha—the supreme and unsurpassed Three Jewels. 5.
I accept the vajra, the bell, and the mudrā according to reality;
and I shall accept the Ācārya in the exalted assembly of the Great Vajra Family.
Day by day, I shall bestow the four gifts six times each.
In the great Jewel family, which is worthy and delightful at this auspicious time,
I accept the True Dharma— outer, secret, and belonging to the three vehicles.
In the pure Great Lotus family, which gives rise to great awakening, || 7–8 ||
I truly undertake the vow associated with all [the families],
performing the rite of worship according to my ability within the supreme assembly of the Great Action Family (Mahākarmakula).
Having generated the unsurpassed, supreme mind of awakening (bodhicitta), [I shall proceed].
I have taken up the complete vow for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings:
I shall ferry across those who have not crossed; I shall liberate those who are unliberated;
I shall give comfort to those who are comfortless, and I shall establish sentient beings in final nirvana.
Then, having first recited [the mantra] three times, the preceptor who knows the mantras should give the tooth-stick and other items to the disciple in this sequence:
a fresh one, twelve finger-breadths in width, produced from a milk-tree.
One should consume an unbroken flower-tip with this mantra:
*Oṃ vajrahāsa haḥ*.
Having stood facing the northeast and consumed it, one should then discard it.
Then the Guru should assign the rites of pacification and so forth according to the directions.
Thereafter, having taken kuśa grass together with its roots and free from defects,
he should cause it to be given to the disciple for the purpose of a bed and pillow with this mantra.
Oṃ vajratīkṣṇa vaṃ. One should tie a threefold-stranded maiden’s thread, consecrated with three knots, upon one's own right arm using this mantra. (16)
Oṃ, Buddha-love, protect, protect all beings, svāhā!

Then the Guru should meditate on a vajra, a lotus, and likewise a wheel, fashioned from the three syllables, in sequence upon his heart, throat, and head. Again, [he should meditate on] that which has been consecrated with the three syllables and well-prepared with scented water.
The knower of reality should cause [the disciple] to drink it for the sake of purifying evil with this mantra:
"Oṃ, O Pure Dharma, purify all the evils of this person; remove all conceptual constructions, hūṃ!"

Then, for the sake of a disciple who has realized reality and who desires to remember the meaning of reality, one should teach the Dharma in order to pacify mental distraction. The teaching of the Dharma by the Buddhas relies upon two truths.

The conventional truth of the world and the truth from the perspective of ultimate reality—non-conceptual profundity and magnificence, the body of the Buddha renowned for its profundity and magnificence: this is known as the two truths. (20–21)
Having understood conventionality and ultimate reality separately through their distinctions, and having then brought them back together, one should meditate upon the imperishable state:
"Everywhere, from everywhere, everything, in every way, at all times, by itself."
He beholds his own self as accomplished and consisting of all Buddhas. (23) Awakening was not given by anyone, nor was it received by anyone;
through the thorough knowledge of one's own nature and phenomena, one is called a Buddha. (24)

The Lord of Beings, having concealed it with great effort, established that reality within the jewel-casket of the aggregates according to the various dispositions of sentient beings. Having understood that through diligent effort by the grace of the Guru’s feet, [one should realize it].
Thereafter, one whose mind is illuminated by reality should engage in the practice.
Herein there is no ritual purity, no restrictive rule, no austerity, nor anything difficult to perform;
one attains success through practices that are not difficult, through lack of restrictions, and through ease and joy.
Whatever evil was committed in the past over countless millions of eons,
all of that indeed goes to destruction upon seeing such a maṇḍala.
Having thus performed the confession properly, one should lie down upon a bed of kuśa grass.
One should instruct them, saying: "Tell me everything that you have seen during the night.
Having heard what was auspicious or inauspicious in the morning, one should further increase the auspicious;
as for an inauspicious dream, one should purify it by teaching the doctrine of selflessness (*nairātmya*).
The Ritual for the Consecration of the Disciple.
[7] "The wise one should mark out with a new, well-prepared, well-measured, and beautiful thread, by means of the meditations on body, speech, and mind. (1)
This is the introductory statement. The detailed explanation of this sūtra is now set forth:
The thread for the mandala should be twice its length, neither too thick nor too thin, colored with five hues representing the five Buddhas, each according to its proper color, yet not overly red.

Having consecrated it with the respective seed-syllables, the mantra-practitioner, possessing the yoga of Akṣobhya, should place it in a pure vessel and offer it to the one who possesses the yoga of Śāśvata. Having taken that which was consecrated with the five seed-syllables, the child should depart.
HŪṂ OṂ SVĀ ĀḤ HĀ.
Having drawn forth the threads with the five seed-syllables, the Guru, who knows the threads,
visualizes them as consisting of five rays and joins them together while reciting the mantra:
*Oṃ dīptadṛṣṭyāṅkuśi jaḥ*.
All phenomena are mutually interpenetrated; all phenomena have entered into one another. Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ.
All phenomena have entered into it completely;
having finished [the ritual], the thread is wound up and placed in a pure vessel.
Having honored it with incense, flowers, and so forth, it is consecrated with the three-syllable mantra.
Then, having arisen, the great yogin, possessing the splendor of a universal monarch,
together with his disciples, should again cast the sky-thread at the conclusion of the wheel-worship.
The disciple and the master, as yogins themselves, have eyes that are the sun and moon marked by the syllable *jaḥ*.
Having uttered the syllable *jaḥ* three times and drawn the thread to the navel,
one should grasp it with the left fist as before with this mantra;
then one should drop it into the sky from the Brahma-thread and so forth, in due order.
Oṃ vajrasamaya sūtraṃ mātikrama hūṃ || hūṃ oṃ svā āḥ hā ||

Having drawn [the thread] with the *vajrapada* mantra, the practitioner, having performed the meditation together with the disciple, should cause the thread— which was previously situated in space— to descend to the ground in that very same manner, being skilled in the ritual procedure. It should be square, with four doors and adorned with four archways (*toraṇa*).

It is joined with four lines and adorned with eight pillars; it is decorated with necklaces and half-necklaces, and features jewels, vajras, and crescent moons. It is inlaid with vajra-jewels at the junctions of the doors and the projections.

The great vajra pillar with a water-pot base and a stepped capital, adorned with birds, beautified by bells and banners, and decorated with chowries and the like. [12] This is the procedure for laying out the thread in space. [8]
Then, having taken up the powder and well-prepared the five-fold dust,
one should indeed cause it to blaze forth immediately thereafter with the *jaḥ*-syllable and the vajra-gaze.
Among the colors such as white and so forth, one should [visualize] each one of the [Buddhas] such as Śāśvata in due order.
Having seen them endowed with the four mudrās and having consecrated them with his own syllable,
the knower of the ritual procedure should again consecrate them with this mantra,
worship them with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and place them in nine vessels.
Oṃ vajracitta samaya hūṃ.
The Ritual for the Recitation of Colors [9].
Then, at the time of dawn, one who possesses the yoga of his own tutelary deity, acting as the Vajra-holder, begins from the northeastern direction with the left fist. 1.
One should fashion the line equally white, yellow, red, green, and blue, divided into twenty parts for the door.
To the east, the paved floor shall be white, and to the south, it shall be yellow.
One should know that the western [quarter] is madder-red, while the northern is green.
That which is the central pavement should have a luster equal to sapphire.
Having fixed the mind upon perfect enlightenment, one of pure intellect should perform everything [in this manner].
One who knows how to apply colors should construct everything— the arches, the steps, the crest, and so forth— using chalk and thread, and with various colored powders.
A thin line causes famine, while a broken one likewise brings about the destruction of life.
Crookedness, departure on a journey, and likewise being excessively corpulent—
whatever faults there may be for yogis whose disposition is not fixed upon reality,
these are never capable of causing an obstacle for those whose disposition is fixed upon the true reality.
Who is capable of correctly constructing the mandalas?
Through the yoga with one's own tutelary deity, the construction of the mandala is accomplished.
[10] This is the procedure for the sprinkling of the colored powders (rajas).
Having accomplished the activity of the *rajas* through union with its own presiding deity,
one should then perform the placement of the *mudrās* according to the ritual procedure prescribed by the rules.
In the center of that, one should draw a thunderbolt (*vajra*) possessing a luster equal to a sapphire.
The five-pronged [vajra], with great flames, is the terror even of terror itself.
To the east is the great wheel, adorned with vajra-flames;
to the south is the great jewel, dense and agitated by sparks.
In the west, one should draw a great lotus with a luster equal to a ruby;
in the north, a great sword blazing and filled with masses of radiant flames.
In the eastern corner, one should draw an eye with a luster like that of the midst of a cloud.
Then, to the south, one should draw a vajra born from the family of Māmakī;
to the west, one should draw a lotus with a radiance like that of a ruby;
and to the north, one should fashion an utpala, beautiful like a dark blue cloud.
The wise one should place a mirror, a lute, a fragrant lotus, and a vessel of liquid in sequence upon the four outer corners. On the eastern plank, he should place a *nāgapuṣpa* flower and a discus.
The practitioner should place a yellow jewel upon a jewel on the right side;
then, one should again place a red lotus upon a lotus in the west;
and the wise one should place a dark blue sword upon a sword in the north.
One should draw a mallet at the eastern gate, radiant with blazing light;
at the southern [gate], one should draw a staff, brilliantly shining with vajra-flames and the like;
at the western [gate], one should draw a lotus, producing the radiance of sword-flames.
To the north, one should draw a vajra for Vajrakuṇḍalī and Vajrin.
In the southeast corner, one should draw a sword; in the southwest, one should draw a noose.
Having drawn a sword in the northwest, one should draw a sword in the northeast.
Having drawn the mark of the *uṣṇīṣa* above, one should draw an *aṅkuśa* below;
having clearly understood the mandala, it is the supreme mind.
One should perform worship with diligence through the cultivation of body, speech, and mind,
having obtained a sixteen-year-old woman of radiant beauty.

Having filled it with perfumes and flowers, one should desire her in its center; and having empowered that Māmakī, whose girdle is virtue, the wise one should emanate the gentle state of Buddhahood, adorned by the element of space. Thus [it is said]. 14–15.

The Tathāgatas, such as Akṣobhya and others, who have arisen from the thought of awakening (bodhicitta), being compassionate by nature, perceive sentient beings whose conduct is dominated by hatred, delusion, and so forth;
having displayed their entire miraculous power and set the wheel of Dharma in motion, [they act for their sake]. (16)
Having purified their hatred and other afflictions through those respective meditative absorptions,
they indeed go to their own respective fields as embodiments of supreme bliss;
there they dwell as they please, longing to return once more.
Then the yogin, knowing the intrinsic nature [of reality], should respectfully urge all the Victors to return once more for the sake of the disciple’s consecration.
And having visualized the subtle gnosis-being (*jñānasattva*) within the heart of the deity...
Furthermore, one should visualize within his heart that which is called Samādhi.
By means of light rays in the form of hooks, produced from oneself and the three beings,
one should draw forth the three beings of the deities in their proper order.
Having thus exhorted and drawn forth the Tathāgatas,
and having caused them all to enter the expanse of space, one should entreat them with this verse:
"May you all come, the sole essence of the worlds, who have quelled the immeasurable and fierce Māras."
The self-arisen ones, who have directly realized the nature of the entire world, possess the infinite nature of the world itself.
(23) Then, by means of the vajra-snap, having summoned those whose nature is the Great Seal (mahāmudrā), one should cause them to assemble within their own symbols by means of this mantra. (24)
Oṃ vajrasamāja jaḥ jaḥ jaḥ.
Having arrived, impelled by the hook of the pledge (*samaya-aṅkuśa*), all the Buddhas indeed sit here in the mandala for the consecration of sentient beings.
Then, the lord of yogins, seeing the Tathāgatas directly before him, is filled with joy.
Having sealed [the vessel] and worshipped it with the *argha* offering, one should praise it together with the bell:
"O Akṣobhyavajra, Great Wisdom, Vajradhātu, Great Sage! O Triple Mandala, Supreme among the Three Vajras, speak the secret; homage be to you! (26–27)
Vairocana, great purity, vajra peace, great delight; teach the phenomena that are luminous by nature, O Vajra, homage be to you!
Ratnarāja, profound excellence, vajra of space, stainless as the sky.
Pure by nature, unstained—O Secret One, homage be to you!
Vajra-amrita, Great King, non-conceptual wielder of the space-vajra;
Having attained the perfection of passion—O Secret One, homage be to you!
O Amoghavajra, perfectly awakened one, fulfiller of all hopes,
born of the nature of purity, Vajrasattva, homage be to you!
(31) By means of this king of hymns, they praise the Tathāgatas.
Vajrasattva himself, the Buddha, stands before one as a friend.

Then the yogi should indeed gratify [him] with the five qualities of sensual pleasure; having performed the internal fire offering (adhyātmika-homa), he should present the bali-offering while reciting this: || 32–33 ||

Oṃ! To those established in the ten directions and to those residing here—gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, unmādas, apasmāras, ostārakas, and so forth—I cause this offering (bali) to be given. Having accepted it, may you obtain happiness and mental well-being; may you make this place free from calamity through the empowerment of all the Buddhas. Oṃ āḥ hūṃ! Having consumed this mass of nectar, may you grant peace to me and my retinue. Svasti svāhā!
The Procedure for Invoking [11]:
Then, having emerged, the Lord of Yogins, radiant with wide-open eyes,
should circumambulate the wheel and begin the opening of the door.
Standing at the western gate, shimmering with the *pratyālīḍha* stance,
one should first recite [the mantra] and open the gate with the *vajrahūṃkāra* mudrā:
*oṃ vajrodghāṭaya samaya praveśaya hūṃ*.
Thus, standing in the northern direction and likewise reciting with a wrathful gaze,
he should open the southern door and release the wrathful mudrā. Then, the yogin, standing in the eastern direction and facing westward, [should do the same].
Having opened the western gate, one should release the wrathful mudrā.
Likewise, standing in the southern direction, one should proceed clockwise as before;
having opened the gate presided over by Dhanada (Kubera), one should enter in this manner.
Then, for the purpose of admitting the disciple, he himself, with palms joined in reverence,
should petition the Great Mandala preceded by the empowerment of truth:
"Vajrasattva, the Great Bliss, arisen from the Clear Light..."
The reflection is indeed like it, and the maṇḍala is also equal to that.
By this truth, may the disciples who have entered the maṇḍala of the mind,
freed from all defilements, behold the entire miraculous power within the wheel.
This is that mandala, the essence, the means for accomplishing vajra-gnosis;
I shall cause the disciple to enter the city of all the Tathāgatas. Through the empowerment of the dharmadhātu and by the recollection of the samaya.
"May all the Tathāgatas grant every prosperity to those who have entered.
Having thus brought [the candidates] to the front gate and sprinkled them with water from the ritual jar,
he should take hold of their face-cloths and bind them with this mantra.
Oṃ, bring the excellent binding of the eyes, hūṃ!

Oṃ, enter, O Blessed One, the city of liberation of great bliss, which bestows the happiness of all accomplishments; O supreme, highest bliss, grant accomplishment! Jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ, may you be fully accomplished! Then he should ask his own disciple: "Who are you, O lover of sexual union? Thereupon the disciple should say: "I am fortunate, O Great Bliss! (12)
To the disciple, who stands with feet together and hands joined in the *saṃpuṭa-añjali* gesture, he should again bestow the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), reciting this verse:
"The Three Jewels are my refuge; I confess all my misdeeds. (13)
I rejoice in the merit of the world and fix my mind upon the awakening of a Buddha.
Then, by means of that very disciple, one should cause [the candidate] to perform the fourfold prostration.
First, having formed the auspicious vajra-añjali gesture directed toward Akṣobhya, and having extended the arms, one should prostrate while reciting this mantra:

Oṃ, I offer myself for the service of the worship of all Tathāgatas; O Vajrasattva of all Tathāgatas, grant me your empowerment! (sarvatathāgatapūjopasthānāyātmānaṃ niryātayāmi sarvatathāgatavajrasattvādhiṣṭhasva māṃ) || 15 ||
Having brought [the disciple] before the Heart [of Ratnasambhava], the mantra-practitioner should again cause him to perform a prostration with joined palms toward his son, using this mantra:
Oṃ, I offer myself for the worship and consecration of all Tathāgatas; consecrate me with the vajra-jewel of all Tathāgatas.
Then, with reference to Amitābha, the preceptor, while reciting the third mantra, should cause the disciple to place his joined palms upon the forehead and bestow a name:
Oṃ, for the sake of initiating the worship of all Tathāgatas, I offer myself; O Vajradharma of all Tathāgatas, initiate me! (17)
Then, having led [the disciple] while pointing toward the one named Amogha and placing his heart in *añjali*, the wise [preceptor] should cause him to take the fourth name with this mantra:
Oṃ, for the sake of the ritual of worship of all Tathāgatas, I offer myself; O Vajrakarma of all Tathāgatas, act for me! (18)
Having said to him, who bears the Sattvavajrī and wears a garland of flowers as his foremost ornament, "You are the pledge," one should administer this firm oath:

"Today you have entered the family of all the Tathāgatas; therefore, I shall generate in you the Vajra-knowledge, by which knowledge you will attain even the accomplishment of all the Tathāgatas, let alone other accomplishments. You must not speak of this before anyone who has not seen the maṇḍala, lest the pledge be violated."
The Guru, having placed that very mudrā upon the head of the disciple, should again strengthen this [bond] by means of the vajra-oath:
"This is your vajra-samaya; it shall split your head if you speak of it to anyone."
Again, having placed the mudrā at his heart, the Guru, being firmly established, should once more exhort the disciple with this mantra of the Vajra Oath:
"Vajrasattva himself is today dwelling within your heart."
If he should speak this method, one should depart at that very moment after piercing [the heart].
Then, taking the vajra-water contained within a great conch shell and consecrating it with the three-syllable mantra, one should indeed make him drink it under oath.
This water of hell shall burn you for transgressing the pledge;
through the preservation of the pledge, there is accomplishment. Drink this vajra-amṛta water!
Oṃ vajrodaka ṭhaḥ.
Holding the disciple by the hand while respectfully offering yellow vajra-water, he should cause him to hear [the following] with a solemn oath, speaking these words clearly:

"From this day forward, I am Vajrapāṇi to you; whatever I say, 'Do this,' must be performed. You must not disregard me, lest, by failing to avoid misfortune, you should meet your end and fall into hell."
Then, for the sake of his own immersion and for the attainment of all accomplishments, the disciple, being composed, should repeat the words prompted by the preceptor:
"May all the Tathāgatas empower me; may Vajrasattva enter me."
Having meditated on the body with a beautiful head, from the soles of the feet up to the crown of the head,
one should visualize below it a circle of fire accompanied by wind. Above that, one should contemplate the syllables *jh*, *jhāiṃ*, and *k* of a red color.
The practitioner should purify his body with streams of light rays arising from that;
having thus rendered it luminous, the adept, for the sake of re-emerging,
should place the syllables *hūṃ*, *haḥ*, *āḥ*, and *i* upon the vessel, the heart, the throat, and the head.
Having formed the mudrā that effects the binding of possession, placed upon the heart of the vessel, one should recite this mantra for the purpose of invoking the Tathāgata:
"This is your samaya-vajra, known as Vajrasattva. (30)
Today itself, he causes you to enter the unsurpassed vajra-gnosis.
Oṃ vajrāveśa aḥ aḥ aḥ aḥ.
If one recites this mantra firmly without entering [the state] in this way,
then one should impel the Jñānasattva with rays of light from the syllable *āḥ*:
*āveśaya stobhaya ra ra ra ra cālaya cālaya hūṃ haḥ āḥ jhaiḥ*.
One should recognize the signs of possession as being a trembling of the heart, horripilation, fainting, dancing, and even falling backward.
Having observed the recipient in detail, one should place the syllable *ĀḤ* upon the tongue.
Having strengthened it with the hundred-syllable mantra, one should cast down the garland with this mantra:
"Stay! O Vajra, be firm for me! Be eternal for me! Dwell within my heart! Grant me all accomplishments! HŪṂ HA HA HA HA HOḤ OṂ ĀḤ KHAṂ VĪRA HŪṂ! O Lord, accept this handful of flowers! HOḤ!"
Having discerned the division of the *kula* from the falling of the flower, the wise one, having performed the rite with mantras, should perform the consecration of the garland upon the head:
"Oṃ, O being of great power, accept this! (35)
The preceptor of firm vows should remove the face-cloth from the disciples, whose eyes are pervaded by the *praṇava* and who are cleansed of all impurities, with this mantra:
"Today Vajrasattva himself is intent upon opening your eyes."
The Vajra-eye, with eyes of joy, opens up the unsurpassed [vision].
(37) Behold this mandala now and generate faith;
you are born into the family of the Buddhas, empowered by the great mantras. (38)
O Vajra, behold!
Then one should reveal the reality of the mandala in its proper sequence and instruct upon the true nature of the thirty-two deities.
The noble truth should be square, with the corners representing the Brahma-abodes.
The so-called bases of inclusion are each designated as "gates";
the mind consisting of the faculty of faith and so forth arises from five ramparts;
and the four bases of psychic power are the fourfold towers. (40–41)
In its center, however, is the wheel which resembles eight mandalas;
this indeed is the eightfold liberation that accomplishes all attainments.
They are always like pillars in the great palace of all the Buddhas.
The Noble Eightfold Path, moreover, is known as the eight pillars.
The symbolic representation of the true meaning of the nature of phenomena (dharmatattva) is the inner mandala of the wheel;
for this is indeed the mind-mandala, the supreme city of great liberation. || 43–44 ||

Then, beginning with the Lord of the Mandala and ending with Nisumbha, the Vajra-holder should show the deities to the disciple as they are established according to their true nature. He should demonstrate the five Buddhas by way of the nature of the five aggregates.
The four goddesses, Locanā and the others, have the nature of earth and the other elements;
likewise, Rūpavajrā and the others have the nature of the five objects of desire.
Furthermore, one should manifest Kṣitigarbha and the others in the form of the eyes and other [sense organs],
and those lords of wrath such as Yamāntaka and Ārya-Acala in the form of the arms and other [limbs];
likewise, the Buddhas Akṣobhya and the others situated in the body-wheel in their proper order.
"Then, having displayed [the mandala] in the outer circle, one should begin the initiation of the disciple.
Thus ends the procedure for the entrance of the disciple.
For the sake of accomplishing the rite of water-sprinkling, the mantra-practitioner should draw a square mandala with four openings in the eastern direction or in the northeast;
it should be two cubits in size, consisting of two enclosures, and in its center, a universal lotus.
Then, one should cause [the area] to be prepared with white, red, and black powders.
Having constructed three enclosures, one should place the four mudrās:
the vajra [...].

Having placed the wheel in the eastern direction, the jewel in the south, the lotus with beautiful filaments in the west, and the crossed-vajra (viśvavajra) in the north, one should arrange the vases.
Thus ends the procedure for the bathing maṇḍala. [13]
Having brought that disciple who has performed the Kṛtamālā consecration into the mandala and established him in the center of the lotus, bearing the pride of the deity,
the preceptor together with his retinue should perform the sprinkling for the Vajra-disciple.
Reciting verses preceded by auspicious blessings while holding up the jars:
"The Victors, bearing the jars, are filled like sesame seeds;
today they consecrate you—knowing this, be well-disposed. (2–3)
I bestow the great vajra empowerment, honored by the three realms, which arises from the abode of the three secrets of all the Buddhas.
Oṃ! By means of the empowerment of the Great Bliss Vajrasattva, I empower you; may you become firm as the sovereign of all Tathāgatas.

That auspiciousness which belongs to the Great Bliss, who dwells in the hearts of all sentient beings, who is the self of all, the sovereign lord of all excellent families, and the progenitor of all beings without exception.
May that auspiciousness be yours today at your excellent consecration—
that auspiciousness which belongs to one who is endowed with the entire Vajra family and who purifies the people overwhelmed by hatred.
May that auspiciousness which belongs to the Lord Akṣobhya, who bears that name, be yours today at your excellent consecration;
that auspiciousness which belongs to him who is endowed with the entire family of delusion.
May that auspiciousness of Vairocana— He who eternally removes the suffering of existence and purifies beings overcome by delusion— be yours today at this supreme consecration. 7.
That auspiciousness which belongs to him who is endowed with the entire family of jewels,
who is intent upon liberating [beings] from the suffering of poverty,
and who purifies the people overwhelmed by pride.
May that auspiciousness attend you today at your excellent consecration—
namely, the auspiciousness of the Lord of the World, who belongs to the entire Padma family and who destroys the cage of worldly existence.

May that auspiciousness which belongs to him who is endowed with the entire family of ritual actions be yours today at your excellent consecration— [the auspiciousness] of the one who purifies the people overcome by passion.

May that [speech] of the Compassionate One— which dispels falsehood by teaching the means for its purification— be an auspicious blessing for you today at this excellent consecration, directed toward those who delight in idle chatter. 10.
Today you have been consecrated by the Buddhas through the vajra-consecration:
Oṃ Āḥ Vajrābhiṣiñca Hūṃ; you and I are Surata. This is the water consecration (udakābhiṣeka).
Having received the water-consecration and emerged from the bathing pavilion,
he should take up his ornaments from the side of the great maṇḍala.
Having put on red garments and being adorned with royal ornaments, [he should proceed].
Holding a white parasol and gladdened by this song:
"O Great Bliss! O Great Passion! O Great Vajra! O Great Wealth!
O Great Wisdom! O Great Knowledge! O Vajrasattva, grant me accomplishment today! (2-3)
O Great Vajra of all Buddhas, bestower of all accomplishments and bliss;
O you who possess all consecrations and all aims, supreme sovereignty of the vajra!
Victory, O primordial Buddha, whose body is the ultimate reality!
Victory to the giver of desire, liberation, wealth, and dharma!
Victory to the great lord of the five supreme knowledges! Victory to the wielder of the thunderbolt, the husband of Mahāśrī! 5.
Thereafter, one should circumambulate the mandala three times clockwise with the guru.
Then, having seated him in the east upon a soft cushion at the entrance,
the guru should honor the disciple with the consecration of all the Buddhas.
Having placed the mudrā upon the center of the head, the forehead, the two sides of the head, and likewise upon the back, one should utter these mantras:
Oṃ vajradhātvīśvari abhiṣiñca āḥ.
Oṃ sattvavajri abhiṣiñca hūṃ | Oṃ ratnavajri abhiṣiñca trāṃ | Oṃ dharmavajri abhiṣiñca hrīḥ |

Oṃ karmavajri abhiṣiñca trāṃ! Having thus conferred the empowerment, [the disciple] is crowned with the diadem of the five Buddhas. Having performed the hanging of the ceremonial scarf (paṭṭa), one should please [the deity] with the *samatāla* rhythm. 8.
Vajra tuṣya hoḥ!
The crown consecration.
One should bestow the Vajra-vow together with the vajra and the bell;
reciting this verse for the purpose of granting the vajra-consecration:
"Take up this vajra, which is the state of all Buddhas, for the sake of perfect accomplishment."
All the Buddhas have bestowed upon you the accomplishment of the Vajra-vow.
Oṃ, I consecrate you as the Lord of Vajras; remain firm, O Vajra, for you are the Samaya.
This is that state of all buddhahood, residing in the hand of Vajrasattva;
you too must always uphold it, O Vajrapāṇi of firm vows.
The disciple, maintaining the pride of Vajragarva and bearing the pride of the deity,
should brandish the vajra in this manner through the samādhi of Vajrasattva.
The being without beginning or end, Vajrasattva, the Great Joy,
Samantabhadra, the soul of all, the Lord of the Vajra-pride, the Master.
Having spoken thus, like the Holder of the Vajra, one should place the vajra within the heart.
And again, one should speak thus as a means for strengthening the mantra.
Oṃ, O Vajra of the accomplishment of all Tathāgatas, remain! I sustain you, O Vajrasattva! Hi hi hi hi hūṃ!
The grasping of the vajra.
Then, commanded by the Guru, the foremost disciple should bring a bell and,
ringing it with his own hand, recite this verse:

Having the form of the wisdom of moon-like radiance, wearing the crown of the Jinas, seated upon a lotus and moon, he who subdues the wicked for the sake of teaching them, the tamer of the three worlds, brandishing the *tarjanī* mudrā as the Vajra of Reality;
sounding the bell of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) which is the echo of *tathatā* in order to awaken the Buddhas.
May that Blessed One, whose nature is the self-essence of all phenomena, be victorious—he for whom everything is utterly empty.
He who perceives [the world] as being like a reflection in a mirror, a dream, an illusion, a bubble, and a magical trick— that one is known as a Lord.
Then, having brought it back again, he places it at his waist.
Bearing the grace of the Vajra-holder, he should recite this mantra:

Oṃ vajrasattva samayam anupālaya, vajrasattvatvenopatiṣṭha, dṛḍho me bhava, sutoṣyo me bhava, anurakto me bhava, supoṣyo me bhava, sarvasiddhiṃ me prayaccha, sarvakarmasu ca me cittaṃ śreyaḥ kuru, hūṃ ha ha ha ha hoḥ, bhagavan sarvatathāgatavajra, mā me muñca, vajrībhava, mahāsamayasattva āḥ.
Oṃ vajraghaṇṭa aḥ aḥ.
I have grasped it, O Blessed One; be present within me.
The consecration of the vajra and bell.
The knower of reality should apply collyrium placed in a vessel made of gold or silver with a probe made of the same material, while reciting the mantra.
Oṃ, Vajranetrā, remove the cataract! Hrīḥ!
O child, the veil of ignorance has been removed from you by the Victors,
just as darkness is removed from the world by a king of physicians using a probe.
Then, having taken a mirror consecrated with the syllable ĀḤ,
he should show it to the vajra-disciple while reciting this verse:
All phenomena are like reflections: transparent, pure, and unclouded;
they are ungraspable and inexpressible, arising from causes and karma.

Having thus understood that all phenomena are indeed devoid of intrinsic nature and without abode, perform incomparable benefit for sentient beings; for you have been born from the breast of the Protectors.
The consecration of the mirror.
Then, having arisen, the Guru, the bestower of boons, becoming himself a Tathāgata, should explain [the initiation] to the disciples, making the disciple of the nature of Vajradhara.
Making the gesture of holding a robe with his left hand and displaying the boon-granting gesture (*varada-hasta*) with his right,
together with all the Tathāgatas, he uttered this verse:
I, the Tathāgata Vajrasattva, prophesy for you,
having extracted you from the miserable states of existence, for the sake of ultimate accomplishment in cyclic existence.
There shall be no further death for you from this Great Bliss Vehicle;
invincible and indestructible, rejoice, free from fear from any quarter.
Today, having utterly conquered the Māras, you have entered the supreme city;
today itself you have attained Buddhahood—of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, the knower of mantras should bestow the Vajra-name initiation upon the disciple by means of a single sound and this mantra, together with the Tathāgatas.

Oṃ, Vajrasattva, I consecrate you with the vajra-name empowerment. O glorious [Name]vajra, through the samaya of the Tathāgatas, may you attain accomplishment; you are the samaya! Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ aḥ!
The name-consecration.
With the jewel-wheel, likewise with the lotus and the thunderbolt,
one should bestow the empowerment of weapons while reciting this verse:
"For the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, throughout all worlds and in every way."
Turn the wheel of Dharma for the sake of the world according to the Vinaya.
Victory! Victory! O Lord of all Tathāgatas, turn the wheel of Dharma!
For the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, throughout all worlds and in every way,
manifest the jewel of the Buddha to the universe according to their respective dispositions.
Oṃ vajraratna, you who have attained the empowerment of the pure wisdom of all phenomena, oṃ oṃ oṃ.
For the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, throughout all worlds and in every way,
manifest the purification of passion for the entire universe according to their respective dispositions.

Oṃ Vajradharma! You whose nature is the lotus-petal of passion, the pure wisdom of all phenomena, Hrīḥ Āḥ! For the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, throughout all worlds and in every way, according to their discipline, manifest the universal Vajra-worship!
Oṃ vajrakarma, you whose nature is the offering of all phenomena purified by primordial wisdom, aḥ!
Having bestowed the empowerment of the weapon and [instructed] the teacher’s conduct according to the rules of the samaya,
the guru should afterwards cause [the disciple] to hear the samaya proclaimed by all the Buddhas.
You must kill living beings and you must speak false words.
You must take what has not been given, and you must consort with the wives of others.
The vajra, the bell, and the mudrā must never be abandoned;
the ācārya must not be disparaged, for he is equal to all the Buddhas.
Whoever should despise the teacher, the guru who is equal to all Buddhas,
shall constantly experience suffering through that insult to all Buddhas.
Therefore, by all means, those who desire the fruit of Buddhahood should worship this one,
who bestows inconceivable fruits, with beings full of devotion.
What state of Buddhahood is easy to attain? Who is capable of warding off cyclic existence?
For whom is there no death once born? Who possesses the power over the two types of karma?
Without the Vajra Guru, one cannot attain the state of nirvana, which is peaceful, irreversible, and the abandonment of all afflictions.
One's own commitment must be maintained constantly; likewise, the Tathāgatas must be worshipped constantly;
and one must constantly give to the guru, for he is equal to all the Buddhas.
There is nothing whatsoever that should not be done with a mind of wisdom and skillful means;
having always become free from conceptual construction, enjoy the five objects of desire.
This perfected commitment and restraint must be constantly guarded by you;
it is the supreme and eternal command proclaimed by all the Buddhas together.
The Ritual for the Consecration of Weapons.
[15] Thus, having been consecrated with the weapons, one should offer a gift to the deity—of three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior, according to one's actual means. 1.

One who possesses faith should, according to the prescribed ritual, offer garments along with jewels— the best, the middling, and another pair of garments for each deity— giving a pair to all of them while dedicating them with this mantra.
Even having performed that mentally, one should worship it with songs and so forth:
Oṃ anuttara-sarvapūjā-megha-samudgate spharad imaṃ gaganakaṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
Then, one should worship the maṇḍala of the Gaṇas with secret offerings, with songs, instrumental music, and dances, and with various kinds of foods and drinks.
Thus ends the ritual for the priestly fee (devadakṣiṇā). [16]
Then one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Guru, the bestower of enlightenment:
the earth, one's beloved wife, and radiant gold and jewels.
By the gift of gems, pearls, and corals, as well as from the gift of one's own body,
whatever is most dear or even more distinguished should indeed be given to the Guru by one who desires that very thing to be inexhaustible.
The teacher is the supreme deity and should be worshipped with diligent effort;
for he himself appears in such a form for the sake of bestowing grace upon the world.
For those who perceive a distinction between the Guru and Vajradhara do not attain the reality characterized by the mass of accomplishments.
Having abandoned all other forms of worship, one should commence the worship of the guru;
for when he is satisfied, that accomplishment of the perfected stage (niṣpannakrama) is obtained.
Because that reality is extremely difficult to attain even in tens of millions of incalculable eons,
it bestows Buddhahood upon one who possesses diligence in this very life.
The Ritual for the Teacher’s Fee (Gurudakṣiṇāvidhi).
[17] Having received the fee in this manner, the teacher, with a well-pleased mind, should grant the disciple the authorization honored by all the Buddhas. 1.
Today you have been consecrated by me with the empowerments of garlands and so forth;
standing before all the Buddhas, you are now freed from all defilements.
Now you are a master of the maṇḍala, a bearer of the mantra and tantra.
Honored by the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and deities— The Māras have been conquered by you this very day; you have attained the state of all-encompassing Buddhahood.
Act for the benefit of all sentient beings, practicing the conduct of a lion.
"O child, you must not practice stinginess regarding any dharmas, nor do anything that is harmful to sentient beings, even in the midst of great perils. Furthermore,
you must not harbor any doubt regarding the various practices as they are prescribed."
Reveal this supreme, incomparable system of mantra practice.
Having drawn the mandala, accept disciples as gurus;
and perform the initiation of the disciples with a mind free from doubt.
"Accomplish both mundane and supramundane siddhi, O you of firm vows!
All those siddhis come to one whose mind has attained the reality [of the truth],
through the empowerment of the dharmadhātu and by the observance of the samayas."
All rites are always accomplished for one who is devoted to the Guru.
Thus you are praised as grateful and a benefactor of the Buddhas;
therefore, those Buddhas, being mindful of what has been done for them, will protect you.
Then, having prostrated with his body bowed low, the disciple, placing his joined palms over his heart, should say "Om" to all that [the teacher has said].
(11) This is the ritual for the initiation by the permission of the disciple. [18]
The maṇḍala of deities, abiding in the form of emanations as male and female, one should cause to enter again into one's own body-wheel;
one should cause the [deities] such as Śāśvata and others to enter by way of the nature of the aggregates, beginning with form.

One should cause Locanā and the others to enter by way of the intrinsic nature of earth and the other elements. Furthermore, the knower of the yoga of the eyes and so forth should place Rūpavajrā and the others within their own respective sense-bases,
together with Kṣitigarbha and the others.

Having placed Yamāntaka and the others upon the arms and other limbs, and having revealed the tenfold reality as it truly is, one should perform the procedure of withdrawal after seeing the entire world-system as consisting of the wheel. Thus ends the procedure of withdrawal. [19]
Having performed the concluding rites at night, at the time of dawn,
one should again collect all the dust and cast it into a river along with offerings.
Then, one should extract the ritual stake (kīla) situated in the middle of the eight directions by means of the mudrā.
Holding [the ritual implement] with tongs while reciting the mantra, standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture:
Oṃ vajrakīla utkīlaya sarvavighnān vajradharājñāpaya hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ hoḥ.
Having removed them from that vessel, one should likewise sprinkle the threads;
then, with sandalwood water, one should wash them while reciting this mantra:
Oṃ āḥ hūṃ, accomplish the welfare of sentient beings, may there be well-being, svāhā!

Then the mantra-practitioner, having fully worshipped the Kings of Wrath with external and internal offerings, as well as songs, dances, and so forth, and having presented the *bali* offering, should dismiss them. Then, having smeared that mandala ground with cow dung—
One should perform a peaceful *homa* for the sake of compassion toward sentient beings and disciples.
This is the procedure for the extraction of the ritual peg (*kīla*).
[20] It is the peaceful state of all Tathāgatas, the abode of all Tathāgatas.
Teach the supreme maṇḍala, the foremost selflessness of all phenomena;
the supreme maṇḍala, complete with all characteristics and yet devoid of all characteristics, the pinnacle of the body of Samantabhadra. (1–2)
Arising from the supreme dharma of peace, purifying the conduct of gnosis—
O Samantabhadra, supreme in speech, proclaim the most excellent maṇḍala!
The great mind of all sentient beings is pure, naturally stainless.
O Samantabhadra, supreme mind, voice, and charioteer of the maṇḍala!
O Sage, there is no other refuge apart from your lotus feet.
For the sake of crossing over saṃsāra, O All-pervading Lord, draw the maṇḍala for me.
With this king of hymns, the vajra-disciple should entreat the Guru, who is of the nature of Vajrasattva, when [the Guru] is about to draw the mandala. Thus ends the procedure for the entreaty.
Having examined many tantras through the grace of my guru and having thoroughly investigated them with those who know them,
I have explained the ritual procedure by dividing it into twenty parts, using clear and concise compositions of words.
By this immeasurable mass of merit accumulated by me today, may all people attain the state of the Holder of the Supreme Vajra;
and by this very fame of my own, may it be shared with Nāgabuddhi.
"May this work endure for a long time as a supreme vajra-jewel."
This concludes the *Mahāvajradhara-upāyika-samāja-maṇḍala*. This work is the composition of the venerable Nāgabuddhi.
These teachings, etc., were caused to be written by the learned monk Jinaśrīmitra. The extent of the text is 730 [units].
